---

Interval data represent **time spans** where something is active.

## How Interval Data Is Represented in the Media Viewer

By default, interval data is shown as a **row of small boxes** in a corner of the media view.

- The row is centered on the current frame and spans a configurable window of frames before and after it.
- Boxes are filled with the interval color when that frame is inside an interval.
- Boxes are minimally filled when that frame is outside an interval, so you can still see temporal context.
- You can choose the corner location (**Top Left**, **Top Right**, **Bottom Left**, **Bottom Right**).
- You can adjust both **box size** and **frame range** (how many frames ahead/behind are shown).

## How Intervals Appear in the Media Viewer

When interval data are enabled, the viewer treats each frame in the interval window as either:

- **inside** an interval (active), or
- **outside** an interval (inactive).

You can also switch to **Border** plotting style, which draws a colored border around the full image whenever the current frame is inside an interval. Border thickness is configurable.

## Temporal Behavior and TimeFrame

Intervals depend directly on the assigned TimeFrame:

- Correct TimeFrame assignment ensures interval boundaries line up with video/frame indices.
- If clocks differ across modalities, use TimeFrame mapping before interpreting overlap.

See [TimeFrame](../../concepts/timeframe.qmd) for synchronization details.

## Practical Tip

Use interval data when you need **durations** and **on/off windows**. Use event data for instantaneous timestamps and point/line/mask data for spatial measurements.
